title: Navigation for an accounting firm
metaTitle: Accounting firm website navigation as a job map
excerpt: Accounting firm website navigation should name jobs in a founder's words and keep one path to book a call. Department labels make them translate.
alt: Hands typing on a laptop at a wooden desk near a window, a working pair of hands in the way navigation should point at the work.
caption: Hands on a laptop by a window, the job visible and ordinary. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should accounting firm menu labels say?
faqs.answer: Use the jobs founders already name, such as monthly books, a catch-up, or the annual return. Department words like advisory can stay internal. The menu should read as a sentence a founder can finish, including a way to book a call.

faqs.question: Where does the booking link belong?
faqs.answer: Keep one book-a-call path on every page, in the same words, where a thumb can reach it. A client login for existing files can sit in a corner. It should not look more important than the call a new founder needs.

faqs.question: How many navigation items are enough?
faqs.answer: Five to seven cover most small firms: the jobs you want, the people, any proof you can publish, and the call. Put careers, brochures, and unnamed article piles in the footer. A mega-menu of city photos hides the jobs.

sources.title: Influencing your title links in search results
How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
An accounting firm website navigation should be a map of jobs, not a list of departments. A founder who needs a calm expert should see labels in words they already use, and one path should book a call. If the menu says what the firm wishes it were, the founder still has to translate it while deciding whether you are steady.

Google's title-link guidance asks for descriptive, concise titles, and it treats the same boilerplate on every page as a reason results become hard to tell apart. Navigation is that problem in a smaller space. Nielsen Norman Group found that the first 10 seconds decide whether people stay, and that they often leave within 10 to 20 seconds. On a phone, the menu may be the only map they open. Vague items spend that glance.

## Jobs, not departments

A department name is how the firm organizes itself. A job name is how a founder describes the year.

"Business services" is a department. "Monthly books" is a job. "Advisory" is a department. "A quarterly look at cash" is a job, if you truly sell that and not a speech. "Compliance" is a department. "Annual return, once the books are current" is a job. "Corporate" is a department. "Cleanup before a raise" is a job.

Use the job in the menu when the reader is a founder. If other accountants refer work, you can keep a professional index where they will look. Do not make it the only menu a founder sees. One site can respect both readers. It should not make the founder learn your org chart in order to book.

Read the menu as a sentence. "We close the month, catch up a quiet ledger, and prepare the return, and you can book a call." If you cannot read it that way, the labels are still internal.

Five to seven items are enough. Home via the logo. The jobs you want. The people. Proof, if you have a decision you can publish. Book a call. A menu of twenty solution areas is a sitemap pretending to be a recommendation. If you are unsure which five jobs to keep, look at the calls you wanted last quarter and name those. The menu is a filter, not an archive.

Order the jobs the way a founder feels the year. Catch-up often comes before a calm monthly close. The return comes after the books are current. Putting them in that sequence teaches the boundary before they open a page.

## Words they already use

Take the words from the last twenty inquiries. Founders say behind, Xero or the name of their ledger, BAS or the local filing word they actually use, payroll, the investor, the notice, monthly. They rarely say holistic, synergy, or excellence.

Match the nav label to the heading on the page it opens. Google notes that titles which do not reflect the page can be replaced, and that the visible heading is one source it uses. If the menu says "Finance" and the page says "Excellence in advisory," you have a contradiction. Make them the same clear phrase.

Avoid a motto as a menu item. The word excellence is not a job. Neither is "insights," unless the writing behind it answers a question a founder already has, with an author name. A magazine label on an empty blog is a door to a closet.

Location belongs in the menu when it changes who can help. "Melbourne, for owner-led companies" is a sort if that is true. "Our offices" as a top item, with no jobs beside it, sends a founder into a map when they needed a person.

## One path that books a call

One item should book a call, on every page, in the same words. "Book a call" is plain. "Let's talk" is fog. "Contact" is acceptable only if the page behind it immediately offers the call and says what the call is for.

Put it where a thumb can reach it. A text button in the header is the reliable version. A link buried inside "About" is a way to lose the founder you just reassured. Do not invent three verbs. Book, start, connect, and inquire as four items is four ways to hesitate. Pick one. The footer can repeat it. Repeating the same action is clarity.

The page it opens should say what happens next, how fast a person replies or whether the calendar is live, and what to have in mind. Entity, ledger, the question. The menu cannot repair a ten-field form. Keep the promise the label made.

If existing clients log in to send files, put that login in a corner with the word "clients" or "log in." It is a tool for people who already hired you. It is not the path for a founder who is still judging fit. Do not let the login outrank the call.

## What stays out of the header

The header is not a shelf for every page you have.

Careers, a newsletter, a PDF brochure, and a partner's speaking page can live in the footer unless they are why people come. A founder should not scan past "thought leadership" to find monthly books.

Do not list every staff member in the header. "People" can open the about page, where names sit next to the jobs. A dropdown of eighteen headshots is a wall. The about page can sort by the kind of company.

Do not spend the header on a skyline, a slogan, or a phone number that reaches a voicemail nobody checks. If you publish a number, write the hours and what it is for. A number with no hours is a small broken promise in the chrome. If the only person who answers is out on client visits, say that email or the booking link is the reliable path.

Dropdowns need a limit. A single column of jobs can work. A mega-menu with photos of the city and the word excellence hides the jobs inside a brochure. On a phone that menu becomes a long accordion. Put the descriptions on the services page, where there is room for the outcome and the boundary.

## The page should agree with the label

When a founder arrives from search, the menu and the heading should agree. Give each page a title element that names the job and keeps the firm name short. That matches Google's advice to brand titles concisely and to avoid a long slogan repeated on every URL.

Mark the current item so they do not reopen the same page looking for it. The booking item stays available even when it is not current. It is the exit, not another article.

Label proof by the job. "Cleanup before a raise" is clearer than "Case studies" for this reader. "Resources" is a drawer with no handle. Use it only if each piece has an author and a point.

Skip a search box until the site is too large for the menu to hold the jobs. On a small firm site, search hides which jobs you recommend. The menu is a point of view. Search is a shrug. Fix the labels before you add a box. If two labels could describe the same page, merge the labels or split the pages. Overlap in the menu is how a founder books the wrong intro and spends the call untangling your own words.

Use the same booking phrase in the header, the footer, and the button on each service. When those three differ, the founder wonders if they lead to different promises. One phrase, one page.

## Review it the way a founder meets it

Open the site on a phone. Ask someone to book a call, and to find the job that matches a quiet ledger or a monthly close. Give them about ten seconds for the first impression. If they open the wrong item, rename it. If they cannot find the booking without help, move it.

Then read every label beside the heading it opens. "About us" opening onto "Our excellence story" is a bug. "People" opening onto names and company types is a fix you make in the label or the heading. Use the founder's words.

Check that a keyboard user can reach "Book a call" without a hover. W3C's WCAG overview applies to mobile and is organized around pages that are perceivable, operable, understandable, and robust. A menu that only works as a desktop hover is a menu many founders never operate.

A client login that looks like the primary button is a review failure. Swap the emphasis. New founders book. Existing clients log in. The visual weight should say that before anyone reads a paragraph.

## After the labels are honest

Photography is the next place a firm hides a department inside a mood. The menu can say "monthly books" while the first image is still a skyline and a caption about excellence. The picture has to argue for the same person and the same kind of company. Read [how to direct the photographs](/blog/photography-direction-for-an-accounting-firm) before you reshoot the header into another city view.

When you want the structure judged as a set of jobs a stranger can repeat, look at [Hanabi's selected work](https://tryhanabi.com/#works). The menu should be that clear.
